newsitem.title: CHINA: HK interbank rates rocket on HK dlr fears.
newsitem.headline: HK interbank rates rocket on HK dlr fears.

text.p: Hong Kong interbank rates surged sharply early on Tuesday on fears the Hong Kong dollar could come under speculative attack, but trade was thin and focused on overnight rates, dealers said.

"The market is just chaotic this morning and rates are high," a Japanese bank dealer said. The overnight rate surged to 20 percent at one point but quickly fell back to 10.00/12.00 percent at about 10.00 a.m. (0200 GMT).

Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) might raise its liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), a key borrowing window for banks, to underpin the Hong Kong dollar, and make it expensive for speculators to fund their positions.
"The HKMA may lift the LAF rate to defend the Hong Kong dollar and interbank rates will jump inevitably," one dealer said.
HongkongBank quoted overnight rates at 6.50-8.50 percent at 9.15 a.m. (0115 gmt).
"If the local stock market behaves reasonably today then the interbank market should calm down a bit," the dealer said.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index tumbled 527 points to 15,559 at the open amid the currency jitters, but erased some losses to trade 336 points lower within the first half hour of trade.
"The high interbank rates (will) help bring the Hong Kong dollar back to where it was before," a local bank dealer said.
The Hong Kong dollar was slightly softer at HK$7.7414/24 to US$1.00 in early trade versus HK$7.7410/20 on Friday.
It hit a low of HK$7.7500 on Friday.
Foreign exchange dealers said they expected spot Hong Kong dollar rates to remain fairly stable, but they predicted volatility in short-term interest rates and forward rates.
Since 1983, the Hong Kong dollar has been pegged to the U.S. dollar at the rate of US$1 for every HK$7.80.
The decision to peg the the local currency to the U.S. dollar was made after a period of volatility in the Hong Kong dollar.
On Sunday, HKMA chief executive Joseph Yam vowed to punish anyone betting against the currency.
The Hong Kong dollar, the last currency in Asia to be pegged to the U.S. dollar, has come under attack in the wake of sharp depreciations of other currencies in the region.
